hookLine: the Nazis take power, and German Jews begin to lose jobs and rights, one rule at a time

cards: Before any fire, there was paper. A teacher in a German city opens an official letter: his post is ended.

Across town, a shopkeeper unlocks his door in the morning and finds a man in uniform standing outside it, next to a painted sign telling customers not to buy from Jews. A lawyer is told he can no longer appear in court.
Nothing has been burned yet. It is signs, letters, forms, stamps. Paper.
Today's title is a year, and this is what it looked like from the inside.

teach.b: In 1933 the Nazi party came to power in Germany. What came first was not violence on every street. It was rules.

teach.h: A BOYCOTT, A DISMISSAL, A BONFIRE.
teach.b: That spring there was a national boycott of Jewish shops, doctors and lawyers, with uniformed men posted at the doors. Then a law pushed Jewish officials out of government service: judges, teachers, clerks.
Rules limited how many Jewish students schools would take. Books by Jewish writers, and by others the regime disliked, were thrown onto bonfires in public squares.

Step by step, much of it printed, signed and stamped, each step a little smaller than the shock it should have caused. People woke up each morning in the same house, on the same street, with one thing fewer.

teach.h: ONE LAW FOR ALL, SAYS THE TORAH.
teach.b: The Torah has a line that runs straight against all of it: "Ye shall have one manner of law, as well for the stranger, as for the home-born." One law, the same rights for the person who belongs and the person who arrives.
What began in Germany in 1933 was the opposite: one law for some citizens and another for their Jewish neighbors, who had been citizens too.
Families had to decide what this meant, with no way of seeing ahead. Some left. Some stayed, hoping it would pass.
Reading it now, you know what came next. They didn't. So today's line is quiet and plain: rights can be taken.
Not only by armies, but by paper, one rule at a time, while ordinary life goes on around it.

how: Jewish communities, schools and Holocaust museums teach the years before the war as part of the story, some by reading the laws and decrees of the time alongside the stories of families who lived under them.

games.q: it's 1933 in Germany. the new regime wants to push Jews out of public life. how does it start?
o: with violence on every street at once.
with a string of signs, boycotts and laws, one after another.
with nothing written down at all.
games.why: it began on paper: a boycott, a law ending Jewish officials' jobs, limits on students, books on bonfires. each step was smaller than the shock it should have caused.

practice: Bring to mind one right you rarely think about: to go to school, to keep your job, to walk into any shop, to pray in your own way or not at all, to vote.
Hold it for a while, and notice who and what keeps it in place for you: a law, a court, neighbors who would object. If your mind turns to the families of 1933, let it, then come back to your breath.

wordCard.voice: Boycott. The national campaign in 1933 against Jewish shops, doctors and lawyers that opened the door to law after law stripping Jews of their rights. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: rights can be taken. In that year, paper came before fire. Go gently.
